book.title: The Organized Mind: Thinking Straight in the Age of Information Overload
book.author: Daniel J. Levitin

chapters.title: Too Much Information, Too Many Decisions
chapters.hook: You have 30 unread messages, and one real decision is waiting behind them.
chapters.counterintuition: Organization is not a test of neat character, but a way to protect scarce attention. A pile of notes can still overload a careful person.
chapters.tryThisNow: During your next conversation about too many options, count 3 claims on your attention, take a short walk, and write one line: "The next decision is ___."
chapters.keyTakeaway: Treat attention as scarce: filter routine inputs before they arrive, batch small choices, and save full thought for the few decisions that deserve it.

breakdown.fastRead:
Serge's message window freezes while a dozen routine requests wait below it. Cassidy asks why he answers each one as it lands. He stops, walks to the end of the subway platform, and writes one line in the saved draft: "The next decision is the vendor choice." That pause is not delay. It is a filter.

Herbert Simon gave this problem its sharp name in 1971. In an information-rich world, attention becomes scarce because each item asks the mind to select, ignore, or act. Every extra input asks attention to pay rent. A full inbox is not a full mind.
breakdown.deepRead:
A boarding pass slides off Cassidy's folder at the airport gate, then the hotel address, baggage tag, and shuttle note follow it. Lucie bends to help. "You had it all in your head?" she asks. Cassidy laughs, then points to George A. Miller's 1956 line in her notes: seven plus or minus two. The number is not a dare. It is a warning label for active memory.

Working memory means the few details a person can hold and use right now. It is the mental counter where you compare a gate number, a seat, a name, and a route. Put too many items on that counter and something rolls off. Later work on focused attention often made the useful number even smaller, near four chunks, but the practical lesson stays plain: the mind needs fewer loose pieces.

That is why filtering beats heroic holding. Lucie does not tell Cassidy to try harder. She asks, "Which details must stay in your head, and which can sit on paper?" Cassidy writes gate, passport, phone on one card. Everything else goes into the folder.

Simon and Miller meet in that small act. Simon explains why the stream costs attention. Miller explains why the mind cannot keep all of it active. The filter line gives the next decision a place to stand.
breakdown.fullRead:
Miles is already copying the phone number onto the clinic intake form when he notices two digits have swapped places. Marguerite, waiting beside the clipboard rack, says, "You read the whole page at once." Miles stops with the pen in the air. He had been holding the name, date, allergy note, insurance line, and callback number together. The error tells him the system is too crowded, not that he is careless.

Roetzel's 2019 review in Business Research gives the broader frame. Information overload appears when the amount, speed, or conflict of inputs exceeds the time and mental resources available. More material can lower decision quality because the person starts skipping cues, leaning on defaults, or comparing the wrong things. That is not a smartphone-only problem. It is an old abundance problem with brighter pipes.

The same pressure can wear a moral mask. A tired person may say, "I should be better at this," while another tab opens and another message arrives. That frame makes overload sound like weak character. The source's sharper point is functional: the display, folder, memo, and routine should cut future attention costs. A messy desk is not the enemy. A setup that makes each paper ask for fresh selection is the enemy.

Leon sees the pattern in a saved draft message. The household thread about a weekend trip has prices, weather, food, pickup times, and two strong opinions. He writes a memo instead of another reply: "Decision needed: train or car. Ignored for now: snacks, playlists, rain plan." Iris texts back, "So the memo is not the archive?" Leon writes, "No. It is the gate." A filter is useful only while judgment stays awake.

This is also why decision fatigue needs careful handling. Repeated choices can push people toward defaults and shortcuts. Still, the evidence does not let the reader treat willpower as a simple fuel tank. The safer lesson is narrower and more useful: do not spend fresh thought on the same small sorting act all day. Put the small sorting act into the world before the day gets noisy.

A good system is humble. It says where a receipt goes, which message gets answered first, and what detail can wait outside the current choice. It does not pretend to know the whole answer before a hard case arrives. When the case is unusual, the system should slow the person down, not hurry them past judgment.

The boundary matters because filtering can become hiding. If a choice involves safety, law, money you cannot lose, or a person who will carry the cost, do not shrink the evidence just to feel calmer. Slow down and gather what the case deserves. The opposite move is right when the missing detail can change the answer. In ordinary overload, though, the first job is not to store every scrap. It is to decide which signals deserve the scarce front of the mind.

examples.title: Frozen Reply Pause
examples.scenario: The reply box refuses to load, and Serge keeps tapping the glass while new team notes stack below the frozen draft. Cassidy says, "Simon named this in 1971." She points to Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World. Serge stops on the subway platform and writes one sentence: "Vendor choice first; updates later." When the app returns, he answers the decision before the routine stream.
examples.whatToDo: Serge uses the stuck message as the pause. He names the one decision that deserves attention, then restarts the thread around that line.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause changes the cost of the stream. Simon's 1971 point becomes practical when a person filters before each message asks for a fresh selection.

examples.title: Gate Folder Spill
examples.scenario: The boarding pass slides from Cassidy's folder, skims the airport gate carpet, and stops under Lucie's shoe. A baggage tag follows. "Seven plus or minus two sounded bigger in Miller's 1956 Psychological Review paper," Cassidy says. Lucie holds up the pass, the passport, and the phone. "Then only these stay live." The rest goes back under the clip.
examples.whatToDo: Cassidy makes the memory limit visible. She keeps three travel details active and puts the rest into the folder where paper can carry them.
examples.whyItMatters: The vignette separates effort from capacity. Miller's 1956 review helps the reader see why a careful person still drops details.

examples.title: Support Handoff Cut
examples.scenario: After the callback misses its window, Lucie reopens the support handoff log. The full case file had followed the transfer, but the next agent spent the first minutes comparing stale links. Roetzel 2019 in Business Research names the pattern: decision quality drops when inputs outrun processing resources. The useful facts were only the order number, failed fix, and promised callback.
examples.whatToDo: Lucie trims the handoff to the few facts the next agent can use. She removes extra links that would force another round of comparison.
examples.whyItMatters: The postmortem makes overload a processing problem. Roetzel's review does not say context is bad; it says decision quality falls when input exceeds available resources.

examples.title: Intake Number Catch
examples.scenario: Copying the callback number onto the clinic form, Miles catches the swapped digits before the pen leaves the box. Marguerite says, "You were holding the allergy note too." Miles nods at Miller's 1956 seven plus or minus two line on the training sheet. "I made the counter too crowded." He covers the other fields and rereads only the number.
examples.whatToDo: Miles treats the error as signal, not shame. He narrows the visible field and checks the one detail he is copying before moving on.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery teaches the reader to respect active-memory limits. Noticing the overload early prevents a small slip from becoming a bad record.

examples.title: Trip Memo Gate
examples.scenario: Restaurant links land in the draft before Leon can send the household trip memo. Leon leaves Iris's links unread and sends the memo anyway: "Decision now: train or car. Hold for later: food, rain plan, playlist. Simon 1971: attention economics says every added item spends attention." Iris answers, "Then we pick transport first."
examples.whatToDo: Leon makes the memo a gate. He writes the live decision at the top and parks the tempting details where they cannot crowd the first choice.
examples.whyItMatters: The written artifact keeps the group from mistaking a bigger archive for a better decision. It uses Simon's attention economics to lower future selection work.

examples.title: DMV Packet Split
examples.scenario: There is not time at the DMV waiting bench to read the whole form packet before the number board moves, so DMV applicant Marguerite circles proof of address, renewal fee, and signature line. Iris keeps every pamphlet open on her lap. "I do not want to miss anything," Iris says. Marguerite says, "Roetzel 2019 called it an information overload review." One reaches the window with three marked pages; the other is still comparing forms.
examples.whatToDo: Marguerite filters for the window's next action while Iris keeps collecting. The contrast shows how more paper can slow the choice it was meant to support.
examples.whyItMatters: The same queue produces two outcomes. Information helps when it fits the time and task; beyond that, it can make judgment worse.

questions.prompt: A support lead receives a larger case file before a fast handoff. The notes conflict in small ways. Which reading fits information overload?
choices: The larger file should improve the handoff because every added detail could help.
The larger file can lower quality when the lead lacks time to process it.
The larger file should be saved whole so the next person can sort it later.
questions.explanation: Fact 1 says overload lowers decision quality when inputs exceed processing capacity. Extra detail helps only when someone can compare it before acting.

questions.prompt: You keep checking each message because ignoring it feels undisciplined. The project chat keeps adding small requests. What would Simon's attention frame change?
choices: It would treat the checking habit as a private discipline problem first.
It would treat each message as spending a scarce selection resource.
It would treat all messages as useful once they are sorted neatly.
questions.explanation: Fact 2 treats attention as an economic resource. The message costs selection time whether the person feels disciplined or not.

questions.prompt: A travel coordinator tries to hold gate, hotel, shuttle, receipt, and passport details at once. What is the safer assumption?
choices: Working memory can keep only a few chunks active for use.
Working memory can stretch to all details when the trip matters.
Working memory should keep the whole plan live until boarding.
questions.explanation: Fact 3 says active memory has a sharp limit. The safer design is to offload details instead of asking effort to remove the ceiling.

questions.prompt: You remember Miller's seven plus or minus two and plan to juggle seven dense ideas during a call. What correction is needed?
choices: Focused working memory may be nearer four chunks, especially with complex material.
The seven-item rule means seven complex ideas can stay equally active.
The classic span removes the need to group related details.
questions.explanation: Fact 4 says modern estimates often put focused capacity near four chunks. The classic phrase is not permission to hold seven complex ideas.

questions.prompt: A coordinator says she can answer messages while building a budget because she switches fast. Which reply fits the evidence?
choices: Fast switching works as parallel work when each task is familiar enough.
Fast switching protects progress when the messages are short and routine.
Fast switching still spends control effort on reloading the goal.
questions.explanation: Fact 5 says switching is not the same as parallel work. Executive control still has to reload goals and suppress the prior task.

questions.prompt: You hear someone say overload began with social media feeds. The group is blaming one app for the whole problem. Which answer keeps the history straight?
choices: Social media created the overload problem because older media moved slowly.
Social media made overload important because print did not strain readers.
Social media amplified an older problem of too much information.
questions.explanation: Fact 6 says cognitive overload is older than smartphones. Digital tools amplified an abundance problem that was already present.

questions.prompt: A manager wants to explain bad choices by saying willpower is an empty fuel tank. What should she say instead?
choices: Repeated decisions prove the fuel-tank model and settle the mechanism.
Repeated decisions matter only when people believe in decision fatigue.
Repeated choices can tax judgment, but the fuel-tank claim is too strong.
questions.explanation: Fact 7 says decision fatigue should be used cautiously. Repeated choice burden is real enough to design around, but the simple fuel-tank mechanism is contested.

questions.prompt: You save every article, note, and link in one perfect archive. Later you still face a crowded search result. What problem remains?
choices: The archive still needs more details before any later decision can be trusted.
The archive can recreate overload when retrieval has no filter.
The archive solves overload once everything has a searchable home.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 says organizing starts with filtering, not storing everything. Retrieval without triage can force the same selection work later.

questions.prompt: A household thread keeps reopening the same tiny choices about a trip. Everyone adds details before choosing transport. Which outside system best protects attention?
choices: A short memo that pre-decides where routine inputs go.
A fuller note file that records every comment in detail.
A shared chat rule that asks everyone to try harder.
questions.explanation: Fact 9 says external systems protect attention by pre-deciding where inputs go. The memo lowers future selection work; a bigger record may only store the overload.

reviewCards.front: When does more information make a decision worse?
reviewCards.back: More information hurts when the amount, speed, or conflict of inputs exceeds the time and attention available. The person then skips cues, relies on defaults, or compares poorly.

reviewCards.front: Why did Herbert Simon call attention scarce in an information-rich world?
reviewCards.back: Every message asks the receiver to select, ignore, or act. That selection time cannot be spent twice, so abundance creates a real attention cost.

reviewCards.front: What does Miller's memory-span work warn the reader not to do?
reviewCards.back: It warns against trying to hold a whole situation in active memory. A few chunks can stay usable at once, so loose details need paper, places, or filters.

reviewCards.front: Why is fast task switching still costly?
reviewCards.back: The mind has to reload the new goal and suppress the old task. Speed does not turn two demanding tasks into true parallel work.

reviewCards.front: Why is a perfect archive not enough to solve overload?
reviewCards.back: A complete archive can push the same selection burden into the future. Without a filter, retrieval asks the brain to sort the stream all over again.

reviewCards.front: What does an external system do when it protects attention well?
reviewCards.back: It pre-decides where routine inputs belong. That shifts repeated selection work out of conscious thought and leaves judgment for cases that deserve it.

implementationPlan.title: Write the Filter Line
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice writing the filter line before the stream takes over. Name the one decision that deserves attention now, then mark which inputs can wait. This is not tidiness; it is attention design.

ifThenPlans.context: When a message stream starts pulling you into small replies.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the stream starts spending attention, then write the filter line: "The decision now is ___." Answer only what serves that line.

ifThenPlans.context: When you catch yourself holding too many live details.
ifThenPlans.plan: If details begin to blur, then move all but the next few chunks onto paper and keep only the active decision in view.

ifThenPlans.context: When you want to save everything for later.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the archive starts growing, then add one filter note at the top that says what the saved material is for.

ifThenPlans.context: When a shared thread keeps reopening routine choices.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the same small choice returns, then write where that input belongs next time so nobody has to sort it again.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: During your next conversation about too many options, write one line before replying: "The decision now is ___." Let that line decide what you answer.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, stage a real crowded-input moment. Before replying, walk for a minute, write the filter line, and use it under the live pressure.

memorableLines.text: Every extra input asks attention to pay rent.
memorableLines.why: It makes Simon's attention-cost idea compact and memorable.

memorableLines.text: A full inbox is not a full mind.
memorableLines.why: It separates information quantity from real understanding.

memorableLines.text: A filter is useful only while judgment stays awake.
memorableLines.why: It preserves the chapter's boundary against over-filtering.

chapters.title: The First Things to Get Straight
chapters.hook: 3 tabs are open, and the task still feels lost. What if focus is not one tool?
chapters.counterintuition: Hard work can still pick the wrong tool: a lost cue, crowded workbench, or hard switch will not yield to grit.
chapters.tryThisNow: During your next first coffee at your usual spot, say to one person: "This task needs a cue, a small workspace, or a switch, not more willpower."
chapters.keyTakeaway: Do not ask one vague power called focus to hold every job; match alerts, cues, workspace, and mode switches to the mental system built for each.

breakdown.fastRead:
Lucas hears the same complaint twice in a class lab: "I just need to focus." One student lost the target, one forgot the rule, and one kept drifting into a daydream. Those are not one problem. Posner and Petersen gave attention three names in 1990: alerting, orienting, and executive control. Alerting gets the mind ready. Orienting picks the target. Executive control handles conflict. Focus is a toolbox, not a spotlight.

Baddeley adds the next split. Working memory is the small workbench where you hold and move a few items right now. Long-term memory is the larger store that needs cues to bring a pattern back. A note is not found until a cue can find it. Good order starts when Lucas asks which mental job is failing before he adds another list.
breakdown.deepRead:
Levi tries to memorize a phone message while another student asks for help. The words stay alive for a few seconds, then blur when he has to compare dates. Baddeley's 2003 working memory model helps explain the blur. Working memory is not a shelf. It is a small active space where the mind keeps items available and changes them for the goal at hand.

That difference matters in ordinary life. A grocery list parked in the head uses the workbench. A rule for sorting mail uses executive control when two piles compete. A saved note uses long-term memory only if the later cue points back to it. Willpower wastes itself when design can carry the cue. Put the library receipt inside the returned volume, and the shelf asks for less from the mind.

A 2008 network-switching study adds one more layer. The right fronto-insular cortex was linked to switching between task-directed brain activity and a more inward default-mode pattern. In plain terms, the brain has help for changing mental rooms. A person who leaves a hard report for a personal text is not only weak. They are asking a switching system to move between outside task and inside thought, then return with the rule still loaded. The practical move is smaller than self-scolding. Name the mental job. If the job is a switch, make the return cue visible. If the job is conflict, lower the number of competing rules. If the job is recall, build a prompt at the point of later need.
breakdown.fullRead:
Frances can make an office look neat and still fail the task. Her inbox has folders, her desk has trays, and her files have names. Then a client asks about the one case she saved last month, and the note hides under a title that made sense only when she wrote it. The problem is not laziness. Capture and retrieval are different jobs.

A bell, a worksheet, and a tricky rule show the first split. Posner and Petersen's attention networks break a loose word into three jobs. Alerting is the ready state, like hearing the first bell before class begins. Orienting is selection, like turning toward the worksheet that matters. Executive control is the referee, like holding the rule when a tempting answer conflicts with it. A noisy room can break alerting. A cluttered screen can break orienting. A form with two rival rules can drain control. The fix changes with the break.

Levi's route card shows the second split. Baddeley's working memory model, reviewed in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, treats active memory as a workspace with parts. The key idea is simple: holding a thing is not the same as using it. Levi can repeat a number and still lose the comparison he was making with it. A person can remember three errands and still forget which one must happen before the pharmacy closes. Organization should keep the workbench small enough to work on.

A lost file name shows the third split. Long-term memory does not act like a clerk who hands over any file on request. It often needs a cue, a prompt tied to the place, object, or question that will matter later. That is why an uncued note can become hidden clutter. The note exists. The path back to it does not. The stored item may be fine while the route to it is broken.

Greta's desk shows the fourth split. In 2008, Sridharan, Levitin, and Menon tied a right-side insular region near the frontal lobe to movement between major brain networks. The central-executive network is useful for goal work. The default-mode network is more tied to inward thought. Those names can sound remote, so picture Greta at a help desk. A caller is waiting, a policy form is open, and a private worry keeps pulling her inward. The next useful action is not to demand a cleaner soul. It is to mark the return path: caller name, policy line, next question.

A stuck task deserves a name before it gets a pep talk. If the trouble is alerting, change the signal. If it is orienting, clear the target. If it is executive control, reduce the rule fight. If it is working memory, stop holding the project in your head. If it is long-term recall, place the cue where the later need will happen. If it is switching, leave a landing strip for the return.

A clinician, pilot, or emergency dispatcher can be misled by this move in live risk. That person may need a rehearsed protocol first, not a fresh analysis of which system is failing. The idea fits ordinary overload best, when the next move can be designed before the cost lands. The right tool beats a louder effort.

examples.title: Back Row Focus
examples.scenario: Lucas hears, "They keep calling it focus," from the back row before his training group starts the worksheet. The instructor has written Posner and Petersen, 1990, Annual Review of Neuroscience, across the board. One learner misses the start cue, one tracks the wrong paragraph, and one cannot ignore a rival rule. Lucas has to sort the confusion into alerting, orienting, and executive control.
examples.whatToDo: Lucas asks each learner what failed first: getting ready, finding the target, or holding the rule against a rival pull. He maps each answer to one attention network.
examples.whyItMatters: The class stops treating attention as one lump. A missed cue, a lost target, and a rule conflict need different supports, so the fix begins with the right name.

examples.title: Levi's Second Run
examples.scenario: "Keep it in your head," Levi's tutor says, and his first try collapses before the last step. The card names Baddeley's 2003 Nature Reviews Neuroscience account of the working memory model. Levi repeats three dates while comparing two routes, then loses the rule. On the second run, the dates sit on paper. Only the route choice stays active.
examples.whatToDo: Levi moves the stable dates out of his head and uses working memory only for the comparison. The changed variable is the load on the active workspace.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast shows why working memory is not a storage bin. It is a small workbench, so notes should hold fixed items while the mind works on the live relation.

examples.title: Frances Names the Switch
examples.scenario: Frances audits two browser histories after the reading group: one task screen, one blank reflection prompt, then a late return to the client file. The 2008 Sridharan, Levitin, and Menon paper gives the clue: the right fronto-insular cortex helps switch between task-directed and inward networks. Her missing return note, not weak will, explains the drift.
examples.whatToDo: Frances writes a return note before moving to the reflection prompt: client name, next file, next action. She treats switching as a real job, not a mood flaw.
examples.whyItMatters: The audit turns brain-network language into a usable rule. When the mind changes modes, a visible landing mark helps it return to the old goal.

examples.title: Layla's Missing Cue
examples.scenario: Layla expected to take notes, but the seminar leader suddenly asks her to find last week's saved passage. No one speaks while the library carrel hums. She thinks, I saved it. Maybe I am bad at recall. No, Baddeley's working memory model is not the store. The store may be fine. What cue did I leave? 2003? Nature Reviews Neuroscience? The tag says only "mind stuff."
examples.whatToDo: Layla renames the note around the later question: working memory, active workspace, cue needed. She stops blaming recall and repairs the retrieval path.
examples.whyItMatters: A missing cue can feel like a missing memory. The scene teaches that capture is unfinished until the future prompt can point back to the stored item.

examples.title: Desmond Budgets Control
examples.scenario: Trainer Desmond slides the easiest practice card into the opening slot during onboarding in the service center. The queue monitor is still quiet. His lesson plan cites Posner and Petersen's 1990 Annual Review of Neuroscience split: alerting, orienting, executive control. He marks routine facts for handouts, conflict cases for live discussion, and start cues for the wall display.
examples.whatToDo: Desmond reserves live discussion for cases with rival rules. He moves routine recall to handouts and uses the wall display to handle alerting and orienting.
examples.whyItMatters: Planning attention before the session protects executive control. The hardest mental tool should go to conflict and judgment, not to facts a cue can carry.

examples.title: Greta's Jammed Drawer
examples.scenario: Greta's help-desk drawer sticks halfway, trapping the paper form while a caller waits on the line. A text about her child flashes on the desk phone. The 2008 PNAS work by Sridharan, Levitin, and Menon puts the right fronto-insular cortex in this switching story. She must choose which loss to risk: ignore the text and lose the family thread, or answer and lose the caller's rule.
examples.whatToDo: Greta writes the caller's name and next policy line before checking the text. She pays the switch cost by leaving a return cue in the exact place she will need it.
examples.whyItMatters: The dilemma is not solved by pretending one pull is fake. A switch can be humane and orderly when the current task has a visible landing mark.

questions.prompt: You tell a study group to "focus harder," but one person missed the start cue and another kept choosing the wrong page. What should you revise first?
choices: Treat both slips as weak effort and shorten the task so the group can push through it.
Separate readiness from target selection before choosing the support each learner needs.
Give every learner the same quiet room so the single attention beam can stay steady.
questions.explanation: Posner and Petersen split attention into alerting, orienting, and executive control. The cue problem differs from the target problem, so one focus order is too blunt.

questions.prompt: A tutor asks Levi to hold several dates in mind while comparing routes. He can repeat the dates but loses the comparison. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: He needs the dates grouped into a longer chant so storage can expand for the whole task.
He is overloading active workspace by asking it to store fixed items and manipulate a relation.
He should use long-term memory first because stored facts are easier to compare than visible ones.
questions.explanation: Baddeley's model treats working memory as an active workbench. Holding and manipulating draw on that small space in different ways.

questions.prompt: Frances saved a client note last month under a title that made sense then. The client calls today, and the title no longer helps. Which lesson fits the case?
choices: The note may still exist, but retrieval fails when the later cue does not point back to it.
The note should stay in active memory until the client asks, since stored notes lose force.
The note proves the memory disappeared, so Frances should rebuild the file from fresh facts.
questions.explanation: Long-term memory is cue-dependent. Forgetting can mean the path is missing, not that the stored material is gone.

questions.prompt: A reader leaves a hard report for a personal message, then struggles to return. What does the 2008 network-switching work add?
choices: It shows the reader mainly lacks commitment, since task return depends on a conscious vow.
It shows the report should be finished only after inward thought has fully settled down.
It shows switching has brain machinery, so a return cue can support the shift back.
questions.explanation: Sridharan, Levitin, and Menon linked the right fronto-insular cortex to network switching. A cue helps the return, while blame misses the mechanism.

questions.prompt: A trainer spends the whole session making people memorize routine facts, then rushes through conflict cases. What should change?
choices: Put routine facts on a visible aid and save live attention for cases with rival rules.
Increase practice time on routine facts until control has fewer reasons to drift.
Ask learners to try longer on every case so the hardest parts get equal effort.
questions.explanation: Executive control is costly because it manages competition among goals or rules. Routine recall should not consume the control needed for conflict.

questions.prompt: You group a long access code into familiar chunks before signing in at a service counter. You can now use it without losing your place. What changed?
choices: The code takes fewer active slots because related details now travel as meaningful groups.
The brain's raw capacity grew for this task because the code became important.
The code moved into long-term memory, so active memory no longer takes part.
questions.explanation: Chunking changes representation, not biology. A group can carry several details as one useful unit in working memory.

questions.prompt: A parent keeps repeating "bring the form" all morning and still forgets after a work call. Which support fits cue-dependent remembering?
choices: Repeat the intention more often so it stays near the top of active thought.
Treat the forgotten form as proof the intention was not important enough.
Place the form by the bag so the doorway triggers the future action.
questions.explanation: External cues help prospective remembering. The visible form moves the burden from fragile rehearsal to the place where action will happen.

questions.prompt: A clerk worries that an automatic filing routine means careless work. Which response best matches the attention tradeoff?
choices: Keep every filing step under close control so unusual cases cannot slip through.
Use the routine for standard cases and reserve attention for exceptions that need judgment.
Avoid routines when accuracy matters because practiced action hides too many errors.
questions.explanation: Automatic routines can free attention when paired with checks for exceptions. Autopilot is risky only when it replaces judgment where judgment is needed.

questions.prompt: A team writes every decision in a shared doc during a product launch. Two weeks later, no one can find the needed item. What did the system confuse?
choices: It confused storage size with team trust, so members should write fewer notes in public.
It confused speed with accuracy, so decisions should wait until people remember them naturally.
It confused capture with retrieval, so each note needs a cue tied to the later question.
questions.explanation: Recording and finding are separate problems. A note without retrieval cues can become clutter even when it was captured correctly.

reviewCards.front: What are Posner and Petersen's three attention jobs, and how does each fail?
reviewCards.back: The jobs are alerting, orienting, and executive control. Alerting fails when the mind is not ready, orienting fails when the target is wrong, and executive control fails when rival rules or responses win.

reviewCards.front: Why is Baddeley's working memory not just a short-term shelf?
reviewCards.back: Working memory holds information for current use and lets the mind manipulate it. A shelf only stores; a workbench stores just enough while comparison, sequencing, or rule use happens.

reviewCards.front: What does attentional scarcity (Ch 1) get wrong if you applied it naively to Baddeley's memory case?
reviewCards.back: Attentional scarcity rightly says selection is limited, but it can blur the next question. A saved note may not need more filtering; it may need a better retrieval cue.

reviewCards.front: How does the right fronto-insular cortex change the way you read task drift?
reviewCards.back: It points to switching machinery between task-directed and inward modes. Drift is not only weak intent; the return path needs a cue when the mind changes modes.

reviewCards.front: Why can writing something down still fail as organization?
reviewCards.back: Capture and retrieval are separate jobs. A note can be accurate and still useless later if its title, place, or prompt does not match the question that will call it back.

reviewCards.front: When should you use the Name the Mental Job move?
reviewCards.back: Use it when a task feels stuck but the cause is unclear. Ask whether the job is readiness, target choice, rule conflict, active workspace, retrieval cue, or mode switch.

implementationPlan.title: Name the Mental Job
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice naming the mental job before adding effort. Ask whether the task needs alerting, orienting, executive control, working memory, long-term retrieval, or a mode switch. The name points to the support: a signal, a clearer target, fewer rival rules, an external note, a cue, or a return mark.

ifThenPlans.context: If a task starts with a vague push to focus
ifThenPlans.plan: If the task starts with a vague push to focus, then use Name the Mental Job and pick one word: alerting, orienting, or control.

ifThenPlans.context: If you keep rehearsing an intention while moving through the day
ifThenPlans.plan: If you keep rehearsing an intention, then use Name the Mental Job and place a cue where the later action should happen.

ifThenPlans.context: If a saved note feels gone when you need it
ifThenPlans.plan: If a saved note feels gone, then use Name the Mental Job and rewrite the title around the question that will retrieve it.

ifThenPlans.context: If a message pulls you away from focused work
ifThenPlans.plan: If a message pulls you away, then use Name the Mental Job and leave a return mark before you switch modes.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: During your next commute, say aloud: "This stuck task needs a named mental job before it needs more effort." Then name the job for one real task.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Ask one person this week to flag when you use "focus" as a catch-all. Compare notes once and translate each flagged moment into a named mental job.

memorableLines.text: Focus is a toolbox, not a spotlight.
memorableLines.why: It replaces the common one-power model with a portable sorting image.

memorableLines.text: A note is not found until a cue can find it.
memorableLines.why: It makes retrieval depend on design, not blame.

memorableLines.text: Willpower wastes itself when design can carry the cue.
memorableLines.why: It gives the practical edge in one line.

chapters.title: Organizing Our Homes
chapters.hook: I once lost my keys under the tray meant to save them; the tray was decor, not memory.
chapters.counterintuition: What looks like tidiness is actually a memory contract. The bowl, label, or shelf must guide the next hand, not just please the eye.
chapters.tryThisNow: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a routine item lands loose, spend ten minutes ranking keys, medicine, and bills by risk. Move one object to cue the top item.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A home helps thinking when places, labels, and containers carry routine memory each day, leaving attention for the household choices that need judgment.

breakdown.fastRead: Julien drops his keys into a bowl by the door, then finds them later under mail. The bowl looked neat, but it did not tell anyone its job. A useful home puts memory into the room: a place, label, or bin holds a small fact so the mind does not rehearse it. A place can remember what a person will forget. In Clark and Chalmers's 1998 case, Otto used a notebook to guide his next move. The notebook was not decor. A useful home does the same. It makes the next right move visible before attention has to search.
breakdown.deepRead:
A medicine shelf with one clear bin does more thinking than a neat row of bottles. Working memory, the few items the mind can hold at once, is bad at serving as a cabinet, calendar, and warning system. David Allen's 2001 Getting Things Done called these loose claims on attention open loops. An open loop is an unfinished thing the mind keeps checking so it will not vanish. A bill on the counter, a refill date, and a missing charger all ask to be remembered.

Donald Norman's everyday design gives the home its practical grammar. An affordance is a visible clue about what an object lets you do, like a handle that invites pulling. A constraint blocks a bad move, like a tray too small to become a mail pile. His 2013 revised edition from Basic Books made the same lesson plain: good design lowers the need for remembered instructions.

So home order is not a contest for clean surfaces. Good order earns attention back. Put the thing where the next action starts. Label the boundary when people forget the category. Let high-risk items, like medicine and bills, get stronger cues than tape, pens, or spare screws. The test is not whether the shelf looks calm in a photo. The test is whether tired hands can still do the right thing.
breakdown.fullRead:
Brooke opens a drawer and finds batteries, a receipt, a tape roll, and one button from a coat. A strict organizer might read that mix as failure. In a working home, the better question is cost: how often will this item be needed, how risky is a miss, and how much attention would exact sorting demand?

Clark and Chalmers help draw the line. Otto's notebook mattered in their 1998 Analysis case because he used it reliably. It stored information and guided action in the way memory normally would. A household cue earns that status only when it is stable. A hook that moves every week is just another thing to remember. A bowl that always takes keys can become part of the route from door to morning.

Norman adds the design test. Affordances and constraints should meet the person at the moment of use. A clear medicine bin near the place where doses are taken gives a stronger cue than a pretty box on a high shelf. A bill tray marked pay this week narrows the next action. A drawer labeled cords and adapters helps only if those are the words people will use when they search. If the label says electronics support, the system sounds smart and fails tired people.

Allen's capture habit fills the gap between objects and promises. Getting Things Done moved commitments out of the head before they could keep buzzing. That matters at home because many domestic failures are not failures of care. They are failures of capture. The prescription refill, the school form, and the broken hinge become open loops when they sit in memory without a trusted place to land. A visible inbox or note pad does not make the work vanish. It stops the mind from acting like a night watchman.

The hard part is knowing when not to sort. More categories can become a second job. Spare screws may not need drawer dividers by size. They may need one small container that says hardware, with a rule that it gets emptied when full. Do not sort what should merely wait. Precision should pay rent in lower search, lower risk, or clearer action.

The counter-case is concrete. Sawyer reaches for the medicine bin and sees the label he made last week, but the pill bottle in his hand has a different dose printed on it. Obeying the home cue would be a mistake. The cue is there to bring attention to the right spot, not to replace judgment when the facts conflict. The same is true when a bill amount looks wrong or a tool feels unsafe. A home can carry routine memory. It should not overrule fresh evidence.

examples.title: Bowl As Notebook
examples.scenario: Parent Julien's fingers pause over the entryway bowl before the commute while his keys still hang from one finger. He predicts another rule, remember this spot, will fix the morning scramble. Then the Clark and Chalmers 1998 Analysis case of Otto's notebook changes the plan: the bowl should not test memory. It should become the memory he reaches first.
examples.whatToDo: Julien moves the bowl to the exact shelf his hand already crosses after the door closes. He adds one small tag, keys only, before the next trip outside.
examples.whyItMatters: The bowl works like Otto's notebook only if it is reliable. A home cue reduces attention when it becomes the first place action naturally goes.

examples.title: Laundry Shelf Texts
examples.scenario: Parent Craig slides a blue marker across the shirt bin in the laundry room before the wash starts while the text thread keeps buzzing. Craig: Detergent keeps ending up with the stain spray. Roommate: I forget which bottle is which. Craig thinks of Donald Norman's 2013 revised edition from Basic Books: affordances and constraints should make use visible. Craig: The shelf needs to show the next hand where wash starts.
examples.whatToDo: Craig moves the stain spray behind a labeled front edge and puts detergent in the open front bin. The shelf now points before anyone recalls a rule.
examples.whyItMatters: The thread shows why visible design beats private memory. A label and a blocked path can answer the question before it becomes another message.

examples.title: Refill Reset
examples.scenario: Caregiver Sawyer is halfway through sorting medicine bottles on the bathroom shelf before dinner when the pharmacy text lands. The old routine is to answer the text, keep two refill dates in his head, and trust memory later. He stops with the cap still loose and restarts the David Allen 2001 Getting Things Done way: capture the open loops first, then return to the shelf.
examples.whatToDo: Sawyer writes the refill task on the paper pad beside the bottles and moves the pad in front of the bin. Only then does he finish sorting the medicine.
examples.whyItMatters: Medicine has higher cost than a missing screwdriver. Capturing the loop outside the head keeps attention from rehearsing a promise it might drop.

examples.title: Junk Drawer Receipt
examples.scenario: The self-checkout receipt was already in Brett's junk drawer before he knew why it bothered him. Back at the kiosk, he had almost built a receipt file for every errand. The Donald Norman lesson from Basic Books on affordances constraints brings him back: a low-value item needs a visible boundary, not a perfect map.
examples.whatToDo: Brett moves one shallow box to the front of the drawer and labels it check later. Receipts go there only until the box fills, then he clears it.
examples.whyItMatters: The drawer is not a moral failure. For cheap, rare, mixed items, a limited container can save more attention than fine sorting would return.

examples.title: Envelope Wall Pocket
examples.scenario: After the rent-week late fee, Trent stands at the kitchen table and empties the hallway wall pocket before sorting the evening mail. The envelopes had not disappeared; they had stayed as unclosed loops. David Allen's 2001 Getting Things Done gives the name for the failure: each bill reminded the household without saying the next action. The pocket stored worry instead of a task.
examples.whatToDo: Trent moves the wall pocket beside the checkbook and marks its front pay or file. Brooke opens the top envelope and names the next action aloud.
examples.whyItMatters: The postmortem keeps the bill from living as background dread. A captured next action lets the home hold the reminder until a person can act.

examples.title: Bin Label Correction
examples.scenario: "If it is not labeled, it is not mine," someone says from the hallway, and Tyler stops filling the clear bins. He has been sorting tools by shape, a tidy plan nobody else will repeat. Donald Norman's Basic Books design lesson on affordances constraints catches him midstream: the bin needs the sorting rule where the next hand can see it.
examples.whatToDo: Tyler pulls the half-filled bin back, crosses out the private shape code, and writes drill bits, picture hooks, and tape on separate front labels.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery matters because shared systems need public cues. A label turns a private category into a rule the next tired person can reuse.

questions.prompt: Julien wants his key bowl to work like Otto's notebook. Which plan follows the extended-mind idea best?
choices: He should rely on the bowl once it reliably guides the morning search.
He should praise the bowl as a useful aid while keeping real memory in his head.
He should remove the bowl and train himself to remember the keys without help.
questions.explanation: Clark and Chalmers support reliable artifacts as part of cognition. Calling the bowl only an aid keeps thinking sealed inside the head, which is the common error.

questions.prompt: If you keep searching three rooms for the same charger before work, which change uses location as a retrieval cue?
choices: Put the charger in one visible home that narrows the search before memory starts guessing.
Hide the charger in a cleaner drawer so the room looks less busy from the door each night.
Promise to remember the charger's last use before setting it down again.
questions.explanation: A stable visible home cuts search by making location do cue work. A cleaner drawer may look orderly, but looks are not the main cognitive value.

questions.prompt: Craig's laundry shelf keeps mixing detergent and stain spray. What should he change first?
choices: He should write a detailed house rule and ask everyone to memorize the bottle order.
He should move both bottles into a closed box so the shelf looks calmer.
He should make the shelf show the action with a front bin and a blocked wrong spot.
questions.explanation: Norman's affordances and constraints make the rule visible at use time. Memorized rules and hidden boxes leave the same burden inside the person.

questions.prompt: Sawyer gets a refill text while sorting medicine. Which response best lowers working-memory load?
choices: He should finish sorting first and repeat the refill date until it feels secure.
He should ignore the text until another alert makes the refill feel urgent.
He should capture the refill on a trusted pad before returning to the bottles.
questions.explanation: Allen's open-loop move gets the commitment out of rehearsal. Repeating the date feels responsible, but interruption makes that internal loop fragile.

questions.prompt: A parent stands by the receipt drawer and wants a file he will use later. Which filing choice fits a functional standard?
choices: He should mirror a full store taxonomy so each receipt has a precise abstract branch.
He should use the prettiest folder names so the file feels orderly when guests see it.
He should group receipts by how he will retrieve or act on them later.
questions.explanation: Functional categories follow retrieval paths and next actions. An abstract hierarchy can look elegant and still fail when Brett needs the receipt.

questions.prompt: A person who opens a drawer after a small repair finds spare screws, rubber bands, and one odd button. Which choice avoids over-sorting?
choices: Use one mixed container when finer sorting would cost more attention than it saves.
Create a permanent named category for every small object before any item can stay.
Discard mixed objects so the drawer keeps only clear categories.
questions.explanation: A low-value mixed container can be rational when precision costs more than it returns. The error is assuming every object deserves a precise home.

questions.prompt: Which plan best handles a bill and a spare tape roll when both lack homes on the hallway shelf?
choices: The tape roll, because tools are harder to spot once they enter a mixed drawer.
The bill, because missed deadlines carry more cost than slower tool retrieval.
Both items, because every piece of clutter deserves equal organizing effort.
questions.explanation: Risk and retrieval frequency set the organizing intensity. Treating all clutter alike wastes effort and under-protects bills or medicine.

questions.prompt: Tyler's tool bins are clear, but nobody knows his sorting rule. What should the next move be?
choices: He should keep the bins unlabeled so people learn the pattern by repeated use.
He should label the boundary so the category becomes public and reusable.
He should make the bins look uniform so the shelf signals care and order.
questions.explanation: Labels help when category boundaries are easy to forget. They are retrieval cues and constraints, not decoration for an already neat shelf.

questions.prompt: You are sitting at a desk where every visible item seems to ask for action. What change protects attention best?
choices: Leave everything visible so the desk can keep every possible task in view.
Remove irrelevant objects from sight so fewer items compete for the next target.
Keep the same layout and practice ignoring the objects until willpower improves.
questions.explanation: Visible irrelevant objects compete for selection. This is not about liking neatness; it is about reducing needless bids for attention.

reviewCards.front: What is externalized household cognition?
reviewCards.back: It is using places, labels, containers, and routines to hold routine memory for the home, so the room guides action before a person has to rehearse every detail.

reviewCards.front: How does Otto's notebook change the way a key bowl should be judged?
reviewCards.back: The bowl is useful only if it reliably guides action, like Otto's notebook did. If it stays stable and trusted, it can become part of the memory path, not just a nice aid.

reviewCards.front: How do affordances and constraints help a home remember rules?
reviewCards.back: An affordance shows what action fits. A constraint blocks or discourages a wrong move. Together they put the rule at the point of use instead of asking someone to recall it later.

reviewCards.front: Why does capturing an open loop lower mental load?
reviewCards.back: The commitment stops needing inner rehearsal. A trusted pad, pocket, or list holds the task until action, so working memory is no longer used as a reminder shelf.

reviewCards.front: When is a junk drawer a rational system instead of a failure?
reviewCards.back: It works when the items are cheap, rare, or mixed, and exact sorting would cost more attention than it saves. The drawer still needs a boundary, such as one small container.

reviewCards.front: Recall attentional scarcity (Ch 1): name one concrete moment here where it actually bites.
reviewCards.back: It bites at the desk or drawer where every visible object asks for action. The home protects scarce attention by hiding or moving irrelevant items before they compete for selection.

implementationPlan.title: Move the Memory Cue
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice moving one object so the room carries a routine memory. Rank the household item by risk, search cost, and use frequency before you design its home. The skill is not tidying. It is making the next action easier to see.

ifThenPlans.context: A routine object lands in a different place for the second time.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the object has started wandering, then Move the Memory Cue by placing one bowl, hook, or tray where your hand already travels.

ifThenPlans.context: A bill, medicine bottle, or deadline paper sits in a pile with low-risk items.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a high-cost item blends into ordinary clutter, then Move the Memory Cue by putting one visible container at the place where action starts.

ifThenPlans.context: Someone asks where an item belongs after you already sorted it.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the category is clear only to you, then Move the Memory Cue by adding one plain label to the front edge.

ifThenPlans.context: You are tempted to create several categories for rare small objects.
ifThenPlans.plan: If sorting would become its own chore, then Move the Memory Cue by choosing one limited mixed container and stopping there.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time a routine object lands loose, rank three candidates by risk, search cost, and use frequency. Move one object to create the cue for the top item.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, change one piece of your space: put one tray, hook, bin, or label where the next action starts. Watch whether search, reminders, or repeated questions drop.

memorableLines.text: A place can remember what a person will forget.
memorableLines.why: It makes the extended-mind idea small enough to use at the door.

memorableLines.text: Good order earns attention back.
memorableLines.why: It separates useful organization from neatness for its own sake.

memorableLines.text: Do not sort what should merely wait.
memorableLines.why: It gives the reader permission to stop before precision wastes attention.

chapters.title: Organizing Our Social World
chapters.hook: Could a labeled acquaintance beat a full address book when the right job lead appears?
chapters.counterintuition: A full contact list can save every name and still make the real network harder to use. The saved name is not the maintained tie.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before you send your next reply, review one recent response that slipped or annoyed someone. Count the miss, then mark whether it was role, channel, or obligation.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Sort people by role, trust, tie strength, obligation, and channel so close care, weak bridges, expert help, and simple retrieval each get the right kind of attention.

breakdown.fastRead:
A swollen phone can hide a thin social system. In Robin Dunbar's social-brain work, the hard part was not storing names. It was maintaining ties, remembering roles, recent contact, obligations, and trust.

Social sorting means grouping people by what the tie is for. A close friend, weak bridge, expert, neighbor, and delivery contact should not pull the same thread in the mind or the same ping on the phone.

Names are cheap; attention is not. The useful system says who needs care, who offers a bridge, and which reply can wait.
breakdown.deepRead:
A reply thread carries more than words. It carries the role of the person, the last promise made, the channel they expect, and the cost of being wrong. That is why social overload feels different from a messy desk. A desk loses paper. A social system can lose trust.

Dunbar's 1992 work in Journal of Human Evolution linked the social brain to bounded group management. The plain lesson is not a magic head count. It is that relationship upkeep spends mental effort. Teagan can remember a colleague's name and still forget the favor she owes.

Mark Granovetter adds the second piece. A weak tie is a loose connection, like an old classmate or former coworker. In his 1973 American Journal of Sociology paper, weak ties mattered because they bridged clusters. Close friends often hear the same news. An acquaintance may sit near a different stream.

Weak ties need doors, not daily care. The practical move is to keep the door labeled. Madeleine does not need to message every old classmate each month. She needs enough context to know who knows hiring managers, who knows schools, and who should not receive a rushed favor request.

Stanley Milgram's 1967 Psychology Today small world problem gives the network a picture. A target person may be reachable through acquaintances, not because everyone knows everyone, but because chains cross groups. The system works only when the path can be traced and trusted.
breakdown.fullRead:
The neatest contact system can become rude when it sorts too hard. A birthday card that sounds like a mail merge tells the truth by accident: the person was filed, not remembered.

Social sorting is useful because attention has a cost. It keeps Brian from sending a project emergency through the same channel as a lunch photo. It helps Jean preserve an old weak tie without giving that tie the same claim as a close friend.

The danger starts when the categories become the relationship. A person tagged expert can still be lonely. A neighbor marked low priority can still be the one who notices a problem at the door. A client stored under invoice can still deserve a careful reply when the work goes wrong.

Good sorting keeps judgment alive. A close friend may need a slow phone call. A loose contact may need only a warm note with context. A group update may belong in a shared post. A true emergency earns the fast channel because fast still means something.

This is why online networks are both useful and tiring. They preserve weak ties with almost no effort. They also pour birthdays, outrage, job changes, jokes, and sales pitches into one feed. The bridge is real, but the noise is real too. Jean and Yves should not cut every weak tie. They should make the useful ones findable and quiet the rest.

A rule can protect care from constant sorting. If birthday cards get warmth, project blockers get direct messages, and broad updates wait for the shared channel, the mind stops holding a tiny vote before every reply. The rule does not replace care. It protects the moment when care is needed.

Milgram's chain image helps here too. A useful path is not the same as owning every link. If Myriam's class can reach a target through acquaintances, then the practical task is to keep paths legible. It is not to demand equal closeness from every person on the route.

The same care applies to obligations. A reminder for an introduction is not fake warmth. It is a cue that keeps a promise from being buried under newer pings. When the cue works, the person receives the follow-through, not an excuse about being busy.

The overcorrection is a social life run like inventory. Every person gets a tag, every reply gets a policy, and no one is allowed to surprise the system. That version is efficient and cold. Social sorting should lower the cost of remembering people, not turn people into entries that excuse forgetting them.

examples.title: Notebook and Phone
examples.scenario: The sorted notebook sits beside the swollen phone, and both came from the same Journal of Human Evolution seminar. Teagan writes "Robin Dunbar, 1992, neocortex group size" under close, bridge, expert, neighbor. Ludovic saves every name from the lecture list. Weeks later, Teagan can ask who needs care; Ludovic scrolls and says, "I remember faces, not promises."
examples.whatToDo: Teagan sorts the new names by role and obligation before saving them. Ludovic saves names alone, then has to rebuild the meaning from memory later.
examples.whyItMatters: Dunbar's social-brain work makes relationship upkeep a capacity problem. A system that stores only names hides the very load the mind needs help carrying.

examples.title: Old Classmate Bridge
examples.scenario: The advisor's marker runs dry mid-circle, and she passes the coach card to Madeleine, who came only to listen. The student beside her is deleting old acquaintances before a job search and calls Mark Granovetter's 1973 American Journal of Sociology weak-ties paper a reason to network harder. Madeleine says, "A weak tie is not clutter. It is a bridge to a room your close friends do not sit in."
examples.whatToDo: Madeleine asks the student to keep loose contacts with a purpose tag. Former classmates, old teammates, and past coworkers get context, not constant messages.
examples.whyItMatters: Weak ties work because they cross clusters. Pruning every loose contact may feel clean, but it can cut off the path that carries new information.

examples.title: Chalk Chain
examples.scenario: Instructor Myriam presses chalk across the recreation center whiteboard while the adult education lesson is still arguing about Stanley Milgram's 1967 Psychology Today small world problem. "I do not know the target," a learner says. Myriam keeps the route moving from acquaintance to acquaintance until the class sees that a path is not the same as owning every person in the chain.
examples.whatToDo: Myriam keeps the class working through indirect links. She has learners name who they would ask next and why that person might know a better path.
examples.whyItMatters: Milgram's small-world image keeps networks from becoming address books. Useful reach can come through trusted chains, not only direct access.

examples.title: Three Message Lanes
examples.scenario: The team chat will not load, and Brian's draft apology sits in the resend queue. Last month, every bug note went by the fastest channel, so urgent pings and FYI comments sounded the same. The reset borrows Dunbar's capacity warning: social meaning costs attention. Now three lanes separate danger, blocked work, and news. Brian sends the apology in the lane that fits.
examples.whatToDo: Brian routes the message by relationship type and cost. He saves the fast channel for danger and uses slower channels when speed would only add noise.
examples.whyItMatters: A channel is part of the social signal. When every message goes by the fastest route, recipients lose the cue that says what deserves immediate attention.

examples.title: Feed Audit
examples.scenario: Two columns sit on the laptop screen. Jean labels the current feed audit "bridges worth keeping" and "noise to quiet" while Yves scrolls through old classmates, recruiters, and strangers. The test comes from Granovetter's 1973 American Journal of Sociology weak-ties idea: loose contacts can bridge clusters. "Then we do not delete every acquaintance," Jean says. "We keep the bridge note and mute the loud updates," Yves says.
examples.whatToDo: Jean keeps weak ties that bridge clusters and quiets updates that add no usable context. The audit preserves access without rewarding every ping.
examples.whyItMatters: Online networks can help and flood at the same time. The work is not simple growth or simple deletion; it is sorting access from noise.

examples.title: Envelope Reply Rule
examples.scenario: Yves turns the birthday-card envelope over, then sets it beside the unanswered inbox. Reply now? Dunbar's capacity problem is not theory here; every ping asks for a slice of care. Friend, client, neighbor, expert. Each needs a different promise. If the rule says cards get warmth and group updates wait, the next response costs less attention.
examples.whatToDo: Yves uses a response rule before opening the next message. The tie type sets the channel and timing, so each ping does not become a fresh social judgment.
examples.whyItMatters: Boundary rules protect attention by removing repeated micro-decisions. They keep care from being measured only by speed.

questions.prompt: You import every contact into one app, yet still forget who needs a follow-up. What should the app help you remember?
choices: It should hold more names so the contact list can remove the social tracking burden.
It should favor the newest contacts because old context matters less than fast retrieval.
It should keep identity, context, obligations, and recent interaction visible with the name.
questions.explanation: Human social tracking is bounded because ties require more than storage. Names help only when the system also carries context, obligation, and recent contact.

questions.prompt: Someone asks only close friends for job leads and ignores old classmates from another field. What should they notice about weak ties?
choices: Old classmates may bridge to information the close circle does not have.
Close friends should stay the only source because they know the seeker best.
Loose contacts matter only after close friends have already found the lead.
questions.explanation: Weak ties can be valuable because they bridge clusters. Close friends often share the same information world, while acquaintances may hear different news.

questions.prompt: You are looking at a large online contact list, but it does not help when you need advice. What is missing?
choices: More contacts are needed because network strength rises mainly with list size.
Tie strength, trust, reciprocity, and context must be clear enough to guide use.
The list should remove weak ties because only close contacts can offer help.
questions.explanation: A social network is not the same as a contact list. Without tie strength and context, more names can add noise without usable access.

questions.prompt: A student says a network is useful only if she personally knows the target person. How should the instructor respond?
choices: She should build direct access first because indirect links cannot carry useful trust.
She can trace trusted acquaintance chains because distant people may be reachable through paths.
She should treat the target as unreachable unless the contact already sits in her phone.
questions.explanation: Small-world paths show that distant people can be reachable through chains. The value lies in traceable links, not direct access to everyone.

questions.prompt: A project lead sends every update through the fastest channel, and people stop reacting to urgent pings. What should change?
choices: Match the channel to the relationship type and attention cost of the message.
Keep the fastest channel for all messages so no update risks being missed.
Move routine updates to a slower channel while keeping speed as the safest default.
questions.explanation: Channels should fit the message. Urgent, intimate, transactional, and broadcast notes carry different attention costs, so one fast lane erases priority.

questions.prompt: You care about birthdays and promised introductions, but interruptions keep breaking follow-through. What does social organization add?
choices: It asks you to rely on sincere concern because caring enough makes cues unnecessary.
It narrows attention to major promises because small social duties rarely matter.
It adds external cues for birthdays, promises, introductions, and follow-ups.
questions.explanation: Remembering social obligations needs support. Good intentions can fail under interruption, so cues carry the promise when memory drops it.

questions.prompt: A volunteer list is alphabetical, but people search by who can translate, drive, or make calls. What would reduce search?
choices: Alphabetize more carefully because spelling is the main retrieval path.
Keep all roles informal so the list stays flexible for future requests.
Add role categories because the needed person is usually sought by purpose.
questions.explanation: Role categories reduce search because people often start from a purpose, not a name. Alphabetical storage helps only when the spelling is already known.

questions.prompt: A reader wants to grow an online network without drowning in updates. Which reading best fits social sorting?
choices: Social platforms mainly expand opportunity, so filtering weakens the network.
Online ties can preserve bridges while also increasing filtering work.
Online updates are mostly noise, so useful weak ties should be deleted.
questions.explanation: Online networks can preserve weak ties and inflate noise at once. The mistake is seeing platforms as only opportunity or only clutter.

questions.prompt: Someone decides response speed message by message and feels tired by noon. Which rule would help?
choices: Set response norms by relationship and channel so each ping does not require a new vote.
Answer each message as it arrives because care is best shown by immediate speed.
Leave response norms loose because fresh judgment can show more care than categories.
questions.explanation: Boundary rules reduce repeated micro-decisions. When channel and response norms are explicit, responsiveness stops becoming a hidden attention tax.

reviewCards.front: What does social sorting help a contact system remember besides names?
reviewCards.back: It helps the system remember role, trust, tie strength, obligation, and channel, so a saved person comes with the context needed for the next action.

reviewCards.front: Why can a weak tie carry useful information that close friends miss?
reviewCards.back: A weak tie may sit in another social cluster. Close friends often share the same news, while an old classmate or former coworker may hear a different lead.

reviewCards.front: What did Milgram's small-world image show about reaching distant people?
reviewCards.back: It showed that distant targets can become reachable through acquaintance chains. The useful path may be indirect, as long as the links can be traced and trusted.

reviewCards.front: Why should the channel match the relationship and message type?
reviewCards.back: A channel carries priority. If every update arrives by the fastest route, urgent, intimate, routine, and broadcast notes all demand the same attention.

reviewCards.front: Which matters more when replies and contacts overload you: externalized household cognition (Ch 3) or social sorting, and why?
reviewCards.back: Externalized household cognition helps objects cue action. Social sorting matters more here because people carry roles, trust, obligations, and channel norms that a simple place or label cannot fully hold.

reviewCards.front: How can a response rule protect care instead of making replies colder?
reviewCards.back: The rule removes tiny repeat decisions about channel and timing. That saves attention for the reply that needs warmth, judgment, or a faster path.

implementationPlan.title: The Reply Tally
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice social sorting before the next message steals attention. Name the tie type, obligation, and channel before replying. The skill is not colder contact; it is better care with less guessing.

ifThenPlans.context: When a message feels urgent only because the channel is fast
ifThenPlans.plan: If speed is the only reason it feels urgent, then move the reply to the channel that fits the relationship and cost.

ifThenPlans.context: When an acquaintance looks easy to delete during a cleanup
ifThenPlans.plan: If the tie bridges a cluster you do not normally hear from, then keep it with a short context tag instead of daily attention.

ifThenPlans.context: When a promise depends on remembering later
ifThenPlans.plan: If the obligation matters, then put the birthday, introduction, or follow-up into a visible cue before the conversation moves on.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next day, count each reply you send without naming the tie type first. Beside the tally, mark whether the miss was role, channel, or obligation.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of the week, review the reply tally once. Name what changed about your social sorting: cleaner channels, fewer missed obligations, or quieter weak-tie noise.

memorableLines.text: Names are cheap; attention is not.
memorableLines.why: It gives the chapter's capacity warning in one portable line.

memorableLines.text: Weak ties need doors, not daily care.
memorableLines.why: It makes Granovetter's weak-tie lesson usable without over-maintaining every acquaintance.

memorableLines.text: A rule can protect care from constant sorting.
memorableLines.why: It explains why response norms can save attention without making relationships colder.

chapters.title: Organizing Our Time
chapters.hook: Can 10 seconds of talk cost the road while both eyes stay there?
chapters.counterintuition: Despite the neat grid, a calendar can still scatter the mind. Time helps only when it lowers switching and saves judgment for the hard calls.
chapters.tryThisNow: The next time you feel the pull to switch tasks, mark "ONE?" on the surface beside you. Ask one person, "When do you need this?" Listen, then write the next block under the mark.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Organize time by placing cues, batches, buffers, and recovery where they protect attention, not by filling every open minute.

breakdown.fastRead:
Beckett keeps both eyes on the simulated road while the phone voice keeps talking. In Strayer, Drews, and Johnston's 2003 JEP Applied work, that was enough to impair driving attention. A person can look at the road and still miss the road.

Temporal scaffolding is time used as a support. A calendar block, a routine, a deadline, or a buffer holds an intention outside the head until the right moment. The goal is not a perfect grid. The goal is fewer costly restarts. Time protects attention when it tells the mind what not to reload.
breakdown.deepRead:
Switching hurts because the mind must reload the job. After every shift, it has to recover the goal, the rules, and the next useful cue. That is why a day can look full and still feel broken. The blocks are real, but each one asks the mind to become a different person again.

Delphine sees the cost in a parole docket. Danziger, Levav, and Avnaim-Pesso's 2011 PNAS study looked at 1,112 judicial rulings and found that timing and breaks were linked with favorable decisions. The lesson is not that judges are careless. It is that hard judgment still runs through a human body in a session, with hunger, fatigue, order, and defaults pressing on it.

This is where time organization becomes practical. Batch similar tasks so one task set can stay warm. Put a buffer after meetings so a late end does not push the next promise sideways. Use a visible cue for a future action instead of rehearsing it all morning. A buffer is attention insurance.

The decision-fatigue debate adds a warning. Ego depletion is the idea that self-control runs down like a tank, but the 2016 multilab replication made that simple story harder to trust. Still, the narrow advice holds: do not spend choice on trivia before work that needs judgment. Save the cleanest mind for the call that can hurt someone.
breakdown.fullRead:
The tidy calendar has a hidden trap. Wallace can color every hour and still spend the day jerking between email, policy reading, errands, and calls. Each switch asks him to remember where he was and what mattered. The calendar looks organized. His attention is not.

The useful word is temporal scaffolding. It means putting time-shaped supports around attention: blocks, routines, deadlines, buffers, and recovery. The support matters because working memory is small. It should not have to keep a future call alive while the body is in traffic and a message thread is asking for a reply.

Strayer, Drews, and Johnston make the danger plain. In simulated driving, the problem was not only hands on a phone. Cell-phone conversation itself competed with the mental work of seeing the road. That finding is why hands-free talk is not a magic fix. The eyes can face forward while the mind is busy somewhere else.

Danziger, Levav, and Avnaim-Pesso make the same point from a different doorway. Their 2011 PNAS parole study tied favorable rulings to session timing and breaks. It does not license a crude claim that every late decision is bad. It does say the conditions around judgment belong inside the design. Food, pauses, order, and default rules can touch serious outcomes.

Decision fatigue needs the same care. The ego depletion debate, including the replication effort in 2016, warns against a cartoon fuel tank. A bad late choice does not prove the person ran out of willpower. Yet nobody needs the cartoon to see the practical rule. If a routine can settle lunch, inbox checks, and meeting prep, it leaves more care for the decision that deserves a human pause.

Good time organization is therefore less heroic than it sounds. Put similar work together. Leave air around transitions. Let a surface carry the cue, such as a sticky note, a margin mark, or a visible file. Place rest before the next demanding block, not only after collapse. Recovery is part of the schedule.

Hannah's fridge note shows the small version. It says CALL, and it sits where the coffee mug stops in the morning. The note is not elegant. It is better than asking her to remember the call through breakfast, traffic, and three alerts. A cue beats a private promise.

The precondition is some control over the next cue, pause, or sequence. A person in an emergency room surge, a live service line, or another person's rigid schedule may not own that control alone. When the precondition is absent, personal time blocks become decoration. The system has to change before the calendar can help.

examples.title: Beckett's Talking Road
examples.scenario: The phone voice asks another question just as traffic swells on the simulator screen. The lab stays quiet except for the road, and the 2003 JEP Applied run needs an answer. He must choose whether to keep the call alive and risk missing what he sees, or drop the call and spoil Strayer, Drews, and Johnston's clean measure.
examples.whatToDo: Beckett names the conflict before the next prompt. He treats the call as a competing task, not as harmless sound, and gives the simulated road the whole task set.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene makes divided attention visible. A calendar that protects driving, writing, or judgment must block the second goal, not merely free the hands.
